title: Mysterious object in Magellanic Cloud may date back to dawn of universe
site_name: BGNES: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
excerpt: Astronomers from Swinburne University of Technology in Melbourne say they may have discovered an object that existed before the first stars appeared. They believe it could be a primordial black hol
content:
he object, detected through a brief brightening of a distant star, is around 100,000 times more likely to be associated with dark matter than with ordinary stellar matter, researchers say

Astronomers from Swinburne University of Technology in Melbourne say they may have discovered an object that existed before the first stars appeared. They believe it could be a primordial black hole formed in the earliest moments of the universe, ScienceDaily reported, citing the university.

The mysterious object, named Phoebe, was detected through a brief brightening of a distant star in the Large Magellanic Cloud, recorded on 18 December 2019.

Over the course of about an hour, the star gradually and symmetrically increased in brightness before returning to its normal level. No signs of an explosion or outburst were observed.

According to the researchers, the phenomenon was gravitational microlensing, an effect predicted by Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity. It occurs when a massive, compact object bends and magnifies the light from a star located behind it from the observer's perspective.

The team is considering three possible explanations for Phoebe's nature: a free-floating planet in the Milky Way; a similar planet within the Large Magellanic Cloud, which would be the first planet ever detected through microlensing outside our galaxy; or a primordial black hole formed from extremely dense regions of space during the first fractions of a second after the Big Bang.

The short duration of the signal, around 60 minutes, points to an object with a very low mass, estimated at approximately three times that of the Moon. This is far too small for a black hole formed through stellar collapse, as such objects typically have a mass at least five times that of the Sun. According to the scientists, this unusual characteristic lends greater support to the primordial origin hypothesis.

By comparing the possible populations to which the object might belong, the researchers found that Phoebe was around 100,000 times more likely to be part of the galaxy's dark matter halo than its ordinary stellar population.

The authors stress that this does not prove Phoebe is a primordial black hole, but they say its possible connection to dark matter is particularly intriguing. If the hypothesis is confirmed, Phoebe could be one of the oldest objects ever detected, dating back around 13 billion years. | BGNES
